title: A Letter from Liora
notebook: Liora has been writing about me for months, trying to understand.
She says I am building democracy where they buried my father.
She called me Mum, not Chancellor.

narrative.text: Liora's reply arrives in a plain envelope with her university return address. The handwriting is yours — the same looping script you taught her when she was seven. She has included a copy of the university paper article she wrote about political accountability, with a note in the margin.

Mum. I have been writing about you for months. Not because I am angry — because I am trying to understand. You govern a country that executed your father. You are trying to build a democracy on the ground where they buried him. That is not abstract to me. That is my family. That is you. I did not need a letter to know you still care. But I am glad you wrote it anyway.

monologue: She called me Mum. Not Chancellor — Mum. That word landed harder than any policy brief I have read this year. She is trying to understand me the way I try to understand the people in that chamber. My daughter, doing political analysis on her own mother. Not sure whether to be proud or heartbroken.

choices.text: "She wrote back. She actually wrote back. And she called me Mum — not Chancellor. That is the first time in months."

reactions.text: She included her university paper in the envelope. It is about you. You read it twice. The analysis is sharp — sharper than most of the briefings you receive. She called you Mum and she wrote about you like a historian. Both things are gifts.
